title: Small jobs with Lambda

story: Late on a Thursday, a run hits a failure nobody planned for, and the code that should give its VM back never runs. The run is gone, but its full VM is still on: 42 cents an hour, all weekend, with nobody watching. Next month a different bug leaves three VMs behind, and the account slowly fills with machines that belong to no one.

Something must notice machines that nobody owns any more and destroy them. It must not depend on the orchestrator, because the orchestrator may be the thing that broke. And it must never touch a machine that is not a sandbox, such as the egress proxy that lives in the same account.
hook.question: How do you run a small piece of code every 15 minutes, without a server of your own, that cleans up abandoned VMs and cannot touch anything else?

read.h: A function, a trigger and a role
p: AWS Lambda runs a function for you when an event arrives, and you never see the server it runs on. Three things are involved. The handler is the function AWS calls, here handler(event, context), with the event as a dictionary. The trigger is what produces events; for the sweeper it is an EventBridge schedule, a rule that fires every 15 minutes, written rate(15 minutes). And the execution role is the IAM role the function wears, so everything it can do is decided by that role's policies. You pay for the milliseconds the handler runs and nothing in between.

Nothing stays in memory from one event to the next, with one exception. The first call after AWS starts a fresh copy of the function is a cold start: Python loads, the code outside the handler runs, which is where the AWS client is created, and then the handler runs. If another event arrives soon, AWS may reuse that warm copy and call only the handler, which is much faster. So expensive setup goes outside the handler, and the handler must never rely on anything from an earlier call.

The sweeper is written in Python, although the rest of the platform is TypeScript, because the infrastructure repo builds all its Lambdas in Python and the DevOps team owns them. You can read it with TypeScript eyes: def is a function, indentation marks the blocks, a dict is an object, [x for x in xs] is a map, and boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python, so boto3.client("ec2") is like new EC2Client({}).

read.h: The sweeper's rule: no lease, no machine
p: The sweeper needs a way to tell an abandoned VM from a busy one without asking the orchestrator. It uses a lease, a tag with an expiry time. When a run claims a VM, it tags it with ai-agents:run-id and ai-agents:lease-until, and while the run lives, the orchestrator moves the lease forward every 5 minutes. If the run dies, nobody moves the lease, and soon it lies in the past. That is the whole signal: a VM with a run ID and a lease in the past has no live owner.

So the handler lists the VMs tagged ai-agents:managed=true, reads their tags, and terminates every one whose lease has passed. The real sweeper has three more rules of the same kind: a VM stopped for over 72 hours, a disk attached to no VM, and a warm-pool VM older than 24 hours, which is replaced so the pool always holds the newest image. All of them work from tags and times only, which is why the sweeper still works on the day the orchestrator does not.

code.file: handler.py (a short version of the sweeper with its main rule)

notes.text: Outside the handler: runs once per cold start, then the client is reused.
Dry run unless told otherwise, so a new version only reports what it would do.
The handler. event is the schedule's event; the sweeper does not need anything from it.
A claimed VM whose lease is missing or in the past: no live run owns it.
Only VMs with our tag are ever looked at, never the proxy or anything else in the account.
One JSON line per decision. Lambda sends everything printed to CloudWatch Logs.

read.h: Dry run first, and a role that only reaches our tags
p: A tool that destroys machines should prove itself before it destroys anything. The sweeper starts with DRY_RUN on, so for the first days it only prints the JSON line for each machine it would terminate. A person reads those lines in the logs, and only then is dry run switched off.

The tag filter in the code is guidance: a good rule that a bug could break. The wall is the execution role. Its policy allows ec2:TerminateInstances only on instances that carry the tag ai-agents:managed=true, the condition you wrote in the IAM lesson. If a bug made the code pick the proxy, AWS would refuse the call, whatever the code says.

deeper.h: Go deeper: wiring the schedule, and the numbers it reports
p: Three AWS calls connect the schedule to the function, and the infrastructure module makes them in Terraform: events put-rule with the schedule expression, lambda add-permission so the EventBridge service may invoke the function (a resource policy on the function, the mirror image of a trust policy), and events put-targets, which names the function as the rule's target. The function is not placed in the sandbox VPC, so it reaches the EC2 API like any client and needs no endpoints.

Each sweep also publishes CloudWatch metrics in the namespace AIAgents/Sweeper, such as OrphansTerminated and VolumesDeleted, and an alert watches them. A sudden rise in orphans means runs are dying without giving their VMs back, which is a bug to look for, not just a mess to clean.

lab.title: Run the sweeper as a real Lambda on your laptop
needs: Docker Desktop running (about 820 MB for the official Lambda Python image)
AWS CLI v2 and the LocalStack image from the p3-1 lab
lab.goal: Run the sweeper in AWS's own Lambda image against three pretend VMs, see a cold and a warm start, and watch it terminate only the VM whose lease has passed.

guess.q: Three VMs: an orphan with our tag and a lease that passed 10 minutes ago, a live run with a lease 2 hours ahead, and the proxy, without our tag but with an old lease. The sweeper runs for real. Which VMs are terminated?

options.text: The orphan and the proxy, because both leases have passed.
options.why: The sweeper only looks at VMs tagged ai-agents:managed=true, and its role could not terminate the proxy anyway.
It is the only VM that is ours and has no live owner. The live run's lease is in the future, and the proxy is not ours.

options.text: None, because the orchestrator must confirm each one first.
options.why: The sweeper deliberately needs nothing from the orchestrator, so it still works when the orchestrator is down.

follow.say: Start LocalStack if it is not running from an earlier lab, and point the AWS CLI at it in a new folder.
follow.do:
docker run --rm -d --name localstack -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack:4.9 && sleep 15
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p3-7 && cd ~/academy-labs/p3-7 && export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
follow.see: (a container ID, or a name conflict if LocalStack is already running, which is fine)

follow.say: Launch three pretend VMs: an orphan whose lease passed 10 minutes ago, a live run with a lease 2 hours ahead, and the proxy, which is not ours.
follow.do:
PAST=$(date -u -v-10M +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S+00:00); FUTURE=$(date -u -v+2H +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S+00:00)
launch() { aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-03cf127a --instance-type m8i.xlarge --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[$1]" --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text; }
launch "{Key=Name,Value=orphan},{Key=ai-agents:managed,Value=true},{Key=ai-agents:run-id,Value=nova-RH-1230},{Key=ai-agents:lease-until,Value=$PAST}"
launch "{Key=Name,Value=live},{Key=ai-agents:managed,Value=true},{Key=ai-agents:run-id,Value=nova-RH-1234},{Key=ai-agents:lease-until,Value=$FUTURE}"
launch "{Key=Name,Value=proxy},{Key=ai-agents:run-id,Value=nova-RH-1229},{Key=ai-agents:lease-until,Value=$PAST}"
follow.see:
i-b15cf3a235585fd90
i-a324be5c1123c9100
i-e7698d47f6c8506c3
(your IDs are different)

follow.say: Save the sweeper from Understand. Then start it in AWS's official Lambda image for Python, which contains the same runtime as real Lambda plus a small emulator that accepts invocations on port 8080. Dry run is on.
follow.do:
Save handler.py from Understand, then:
docker run -d --rm --name sweeper -p 9000:8080 -v "$PWD:/var/task:ro" -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test -e AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 -e AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://host.docker.internal:4566 -e DRY_RUN=true public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.13 handler.handler
follow.see: (a container ID; the first time, Docker also downloads the image)

follow.say: Invoke it the way the EventBridge schedule would, with a scheduled event, then read its log.
follow.do:
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9000/2015-03-31/functions/function/invocations -d '{"source": "aws.events", "detail-type": "Scheduled Event"}'; echo
docker logs sweeper 2>&1 | grep -E 'action|REPORT'

follow.say: Invoke it again at once. This time the warm copy is reused: Python, boto3 and the EC2 client are already loaded.
follow.do:
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9000/2015-03-31/functions/function/invocations -d '{"source": "aws.events", "detail-type": "Scheduled Event"}'; echo
docker logs sweeper 2>&1 | grep REPORT | tail -1
follow.see:
{"swept": 1, "dry_run": true}
REPORT RequestId: 5d7c55fa-f2f0-4cad-84f8-692701760747	Duration: 6.22 ms	Billed Duration: 7 ms	…

follow.say: Dry run changed nothing, so all three VMs still run. Read the log, agree with it, then restart the function with dry run off and invoke it once more.
follow.do:
aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[Tags[?Key==`Name`]|[0].Value, State.Name]' --output text
docker rm -f sweeper && docker run -d --rm --name sweeper -p 9000:8080 -v "$PWD:/var/task:ro" -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test -e AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 -e AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://host.docker.internal:4566 -e DRY_RUN=false public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.13 handler.handler
sleep 3 && curl -s -X POST http://localhost:9000/2015-03-31/functions/function/invocations -d '{"source": "aws.events", "detail-type": "Scheduled Event"}'; echo
aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[Tags[?Key==`Name`]|[0].Value, State.Name]' --output text

orphan	running
live	running
proxy	running
…
{"swept": 1, "dry_run": false}
orphan	terminated
live	running
proxy	running

lab.build: Add the orphaned-disk rule. A disk (an EBS volume) that belongs to a finished run and is attached to no VM shows the status available. Add a function that lists volumes tagged ai-agents:managed=true with the status available, and make the handler delete each one through the same act() logging, so a dry run reports it first. Create two test disks in LocalStack, one tagged and one not (aws ec2 create-volume --availability-zone us-east-1a --size 120, with --tag-specifications for the tagged one), restart the function with dry run off, invoke it, and run aws ec2 describe-volumes to confirm that only the tagged disk is gone.
checks: The dry-run invocation returns {"swept": 1, "dry_run": true} and logs one terminate line, for the orphan.
The second invocation's REPORT shows a much shorter duration than the first: a warm start.
After the real run, the orphan is terminated and the live VM and the proxy still run.
Your new rule deletes the tagged available disk and leaves the untagged one.
You stopped the function (docker stop sweeper) and LocalStack (docker stop localstack).
lab.fix: A teammate removed MANAGED from the instance filter "to catch more orphans". Make the same change, so the filter is only [{"Name": "instance-state-name", ...}], and launch a fresh proxy-like VM with an old lease (the third launch line from step 2). Restart the function with DRY_RUN=true and invoke it: the log now plans to terminate the proxy. Put the filter back. Then answer: if this version had run with dry run off in the real account, what would have stopped it, and why do we still want the filter in the code?
explain: Why does the sweeper decide from tags and lease times instead of asking the orchestrator which runs are alive?
What runs during a cold start that does not run on a warm call, and why does the EC2 client sit outside the handler?
The code filters on ai-agents:managed=true and so does the execution role's condition. Which one is the wall, and what is the other one for?
lab.done: The sweeper's dry run reports only the orphan, the real run terminates only the orphan, your disk rule deletes only the tagged disk, and nothing is left running.

check.q: The orchestrator has been down for an hour. What does the sweeper do with the VMs of runs that were in flight?

options.text: Nothing, because it waits for the orchestrator to say which runs are alive
options.why: The sweeper never asks the orchestrator. It works from tags so it can work when the orchestrator cannot.

options.text: It terminates every running VM to be safe
options.why: It terminates only VMs whose lease has passed. A VM with a lease in the future is left alone.

options.text: Their leases stop moving, and once a lease passes, the sweeper terminates that VM on its next 15-minute run
options.why: The lease is the only signal it needs: no one moving it forward means no live owner.

check.q: Why does the sweeper create its EC2 client outside the handler?

options.text: Because code outside the handler runs once per cold start, and warm calls reuse the client
options.why: Setup that is the same for every call belongs outside, so warm calls skip it. The handler itself must not depend on earlier calls.

options.text: Because the handler is not allowed to create AWS clients
options.why: It could, but then every call would pay for it again.

options.text: Because the client keeps the list of VMs from the last run
options.why: Nothing from an earlier call can be trusted to be there; each sweep lists the VMs again.

check.q: A bug makes the sweeper try to terminate the egress proxy, which has no ai-agents:managed tag. What happens with our setup?

options.text: The proxy is terminated, because the sweeper's role can terminate instances
options.why: The role can terminate instances only when they carry ai-agents:managed=true.

options.text: AWS refuses the call, because the execution role's condition requires our tag
options.why: The code's filter is guidance that a bug can break; the role's condition is the wall that holds anyway.

options.text: Lambda refuses to run code with bugs
options.why: Lambda runs whatever you deploy. Safety comes from the role, not from the runtime.

p: The sweeper is a module in the infrastructure repo, copied from the existing Lambda that stops developers' VMs on a schedule: a Python Lambda on an EventBridge schedule of rate(15 minutes), not attached to any VPC, with an execution role that can terminate instances and delete volumes only when they carry ai-agents:managed=true. It starts with dry run on and logs one JSON line per action.

Its rules: a claimed VM whose lease has passed, a VM stopped for over 72 hours, an orphaned disk, and a warm-pool VM older than 24 hours. The orchestrator renews each claimed VM's lease every 5 minutes, and a parked VM gets a lease of 73 hours. The sweeper's metrics feed the platform's alerts, and the account's vCPU quotas are the final limit behind it.

tickets.why: The sweeper Lambda: its rules, the dry run, the tag-scoped role and the AIAgents/Sweeper metrics.
Renews the lease while a run lives, and sets the 73-hour lease on a parked VM.
The alerts that read the sweeper's metrics.

words.plain: Code that AWS runs when an event arrives, on servers you never see; you pay for the milliseconds it runs.
The function AWS calls for each event, such as handler(event, context).
The first call to a fresh copy of the function, which also runs the code outside the handler; later warm calls skip it.
The IAM role a Lambda function wears; it decides everything the function can do.
A rule that sends an event on a timetable, such as rate(15 minutes), to a target like a Lambda function.
A tag with an expiry time that a live run keeps moving forward; a lease in the past means no live owner.

review.q: Name the three things a Lambda function needs, using the sweeper as the example.
review.a: A handler (handler(event, context) in handler.py), a trigger (an EventBridge schedule, rate(15 minutes)) and an execution role (terminate only instances tagged ai-agents:managed=true).

review.q: Explain how a lease lets the sweeper find abandoned VMs without asking the orchestrator.
review.a: A claimed VM carries ai-agents:lease-until, which the orchestrator moves forward every 5 minutes while the run lives. If the run dies, the lease stops moving and passes, and the sweeper terminates any of our VMs with a run ID and a lease in the past.

review.q: Why does a new sweeper version start with DRY_RUN on?
review.a: A tool that destroys machines should first show what it would do. People read its JSON lines in the logs, and only then is dry run turned off.

remember: A Lambda is a handler, a trigger and a role: the sweeper runs every 15 minutes, terminates our VMs whose lease has passed, and its role makes sure it can touch nothing else.
